settings.about_hint: It asks your UPS over SNMP how it is doing — either a UPS with its own network card, or a USB UPS relayed by a Synology NAS.
settings.prereq_synology: Synology: enable SNMP in DSM (Control Panel → Terminal & SNMP, SNMPv1/v2c), and set the UPS up under Hardware & Power → UPS.
settings.prereq_card: UPS network card: SNMP is off by default on recent APC NMC firmware. Turn SNMPv1 on and leave the community as "public", otherwise a network sweep cannot see it.
settings.prereq_nut: A plain Linux box running NUT exposes nothing over SNMP, and is not supported.
settings.scan_hint: Sweeps your subnet and reports every address that answers, so you can tell an address that is silent from one that is reachable but has SNMP switched off. Nothing is added to Homey from this page — use Add device for that.
settings.scan_none: No SNMP device answered. That almost always means SNMP is still switched off rather than that nothing is there — see the list above.
settings.scan_unavailable: This build of the app has no sweep endpoint yet.
settings.probe_hint: Ask a single address directly. Use it when you already know where the UPS is and the sweep still comes up empty.
settings.probe_no_snmp: {{host}} is reachable, but does not answer over SNMP. The service is almost certainly switched off — see what to enable above.
settings.probe_silent: {{host}} did not answer at all. Check the address, or that the device is powered on.
settings.trace_hint: What the app has been doing, most recent last. Attach this to a bug report — an app installed from the CLI has no log anywhere else.
settings.trace_off: No trace buffer is attached, so nothing is being recorded.

pair.title: Find your UPS
pair.intro: Homey will sweep your network for devices that answer over SNMP — a UPS with its own network card, or a Synology NAS relaying a USB UPS.
pair.scanning_slow: A full sweep takes about fifteen seconds.
pair.manual_hint: Use this if the sweep found nothing but you know where the device is.
pair.empty_title: Nothing answered over SNMP — here is what to switch on
pair.empty_lead: An empty list nearly always means SNMP is still switched off, not that there is no UPS. Both supported paths need you to enable something first.
pair.empty_synology: Synology NAS relaying a USB UPS: Control Panel → Terminal & SNMP → tick SNMP service and SNMPv1/v2c. Then Hardware & Power → UPS → enable UPS support.
pair.empty_card: UPS with its own network card: on recent APC NMC firmware SNMP ships switched off, v1 and v3 alike. In the card's web interface, Configuration → Network → SNMPv1 → enable it, and leave the community as "public".
pair.empty_nut: A plain Linux machine running NUT is not supported: NUT has no SNMP agent, so there is nothing here to find.
pair.empty_retry: Switch it on, then search again.
pair.reachable_lead: These addresses answered a ping but not an SNMP request. That is the signature of SNMP being switched off on a device that is otherwise perfectly healthy.
pair.repair_title: Point this device at a new address
pair.repair_hint: Use this when the UPS — or the NAS relaying it — moved to a different IP address. Reserve a fixed address in your router to stop it happening again.
pair.repair_mismatch: That address answers, but it is a different UPS ({{found}} instead of {{expected}}). Nothing was changed.

pair_nas.title: Find your NAS
pair_nas.intro: Homey will sweep your network for machines that publish HOST-RESOURCES-MIB over SNMP — a Synology, a QNAP, a Linux box running snmpd, an ESXi host.
pair_nas.not_readable: that address answered, but nothing on it could be read
pair_nas.others_title: SNMP works here, but no host answered
pair_nas.others_lead: These addresses answered SNMP but do not publish HOST-RESOURCES-MIB — or publish it without a single readable measurement. So SNMP itself is fine on your network; it is this particular machine that is not serving the host MIB.
pair_nas.empty_title: Nothing answered over SNMP — here is what to switch on
pair_nas.empty_lead: An empty list nearly always means SNMP is still switched off, not that there is no NAS. Every supported path needs you to enable something first.
pair_nas.empty_synology: Synology: Control Panel → Terminal & SNMP → tick “Enable SNMP service” and SNMPv1/v2c, and leave the community as "public".
pair_nas.empty_qnap: QNAP: Control Panel → Network & File Services → SNMP → enable the SNMP service, version 1/2.
pair_nas.empty_linux: Linux: install and start snmpd, then make sure it listens on the LAN — the packaged configuration binds to 127.0.0.1 only, so it answers the machine itself and nobody else.
pair_nas.repair_hint: Use this when the host moved to a different IP address. Reserve a fixed address in your router to stop it happening again.
pair_nas.repair_mismatch: That address answers, but it is a different host ({{found}} instead of {{expected}}). Nothing was changed.
